rows.source: HSE molten metals and foundry health risks
rows.verified: Sand handling, fettling and kiln-relining materials can generate respirable crystalline silica when dry.

rows.source: HSE molten metals and foundry health risks
rows.verified: Inhaling respirable crystalline silica can cause silicosis, a serious and irreversible lung disease.

rows.source: HSE molten metals and foundry health risks
rows.verified: Ferrous foundry fume can cause lung cancer.

rows.source: HSE molten metals and foundry health risks
rows.verified: Pattern-assembly fume and spray mists can cause occupational asthma and other lung disease.

rows.source: HSE molten metals and foundry health risks
rows.verified: COSHH requires employers to protect workers from hazardous foundry dust and fume.

rows.source: HSE molten metals and foundry health risks
rows.verified: Dust and fume controls should be kept in good working order and their continued effectiveness demonstrated through records and monitoring.

rows.source: HSE molten metals and foundry health risks
rows.verified: Foundry manual-handling risks can be assessed using HSE tools for lifting, repetitive work, pushing and pulling.

rows.source: HSE molten metals and foundry health risks
rows.verified: Hand-held powered tools can expose foundry workers to hand-arm vibration, which employers must prevent or reduce.

rows.source: HSE molten metals and foundry health risks
rows.verified: Foundry risk depends on alloy, process, sand system, temperature, enclosure, extraction, task duration, maintenance and worker susceptibility.

rows.source: HSE molten metals and foundry health risks
rows.verified: Foundry evidence is process-, material-, exposure- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level illness or injury probability.

rows.source: HSE ceramics and silica controls
rows.verified: Common ceramics injuries include handling or lifting injuries, slips and trips, impacts from moving or falling objects and contact with moving machinery.

rows.source: HSE ceramics and silica controls
rows.verified: Common occupational ill health in ceramics includes musculoskeletal disorders and dermatitis.

rows.source: HSE ceramics and silica controls
rows.verified: HSE ceramics COSHH guidance is intended to control exposure to respirable crystalline silica.

rows.source: HSE ceramics and silica controls
rows.verified: Glaze and colour preparation controls cover weighing powders and mixing them into water-based preparations.

rows.source: HSE ceramics and silica controls
rows.verified: Kiln loading and unloading require controls that reduce silica exposure to an adequate level.

rows.source: HSE ceramics and silica controls
rows.verified: Spraying glazes and colours requires effective exposure controls and may require air sampling and engineering-control checks.

rows.source: HSE ceramics and silica controls
rows.verified: Related ceramics controls include health surveillance for occupational dermatitis and respirable crystalline silica exposure.

rows.source: HSE ceramics and silica controls
rows.verified: Health surveillance must be provided where workers are regularly exposed to RCS and there is a reasonable likelihood that silicosis may develop.

rows.source: HSE ceramics and silica controls
rows.verified: Ceramics risk depends on raw materials, silica content, process dryness, glaze composition, kiln task, ventilation, housekeeping and exposure duration.

rows.source: HSE ceramics and silica controls
rows.verified: Ceramics evidence is material-, process-, exposure- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level disease or injury probability.
